title: Rome’s three eras
description: Roman history runs from the Kingdom to the Republic (509 BCE) to the Empire (27 BCE); the West fell in 476 CE and the East in 1453.

facts.text: Roman history is usually divided into the Kingdom, the Republic (from 509 BCE) and the Empire (from 27 BCE).
The last emperor in the West, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed in 476 CE, the usual date given for the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
The eastern half of the empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until the city fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.
Roman tradition dated the founding of Rome to 753 BCE.

title: An empire around a sea
description: At its height Rome ruled every coast of the Mediterranean, which Romans called “our sea.”

facts.text: At its height the Roman Empire surrounded the Mediterranean, stretching from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the Middle East.
Romans called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.”

title: Romulus and Remus
description: Rome’s founding legend: twins raised by a she-wolf, a fratricide, and a city named for Romulus.

facts.text: According to legend, Rome was founded by the twins Romulus and Remus, sons of the god Mars, who were abandoned as babies and nursed by a she-wolf.
The she-wolf nursing the twins became one of Rome’s best-known symbols.
In the legend, Romulus killed Remus in a quarrel over the new city, which was named after Romulus.
Romans also traced their ancestry to Aeneas, a Trojan prince who, in legend, fled the fall of Troy to Italy.
Historians treat Rome’s founding stories as legend: they were written down centuries after the events they describe.

title: Rome’s first villages
description: Archaeology shows Latin hilltop villages from about the 8th century BCE that merged into a town around a drained valley, the Forum.

facts.text: The first Romans were Latins, a people of the region of Latium in central Italy.
Archaeologists have found traces of Iron Age huts on the Palatine Hill from around the 8th century BCE, close to the traditional founding date.
Early Rome grew from small hilltop villages that gradually merged into one community.
The valley that became the Roman Forum was once marshy and was drained, helped by the great drain later called the Cloaca Maxima.
Parts of the Cloaca Maxima still carry water today.

title: Seven hills and a river
description: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on defensible hills, with Ostia as its port.

facts.text: Rome grew where the Tiber River could be crossed, near an island in the river, about 25 km from the sea.
An ancient salt route, later called the Via Salaria, passed through Rome’s site, linking the coast with inland Italy.
Ancient Rome was built on seven hills beside the Tiber, among them the Palatine and the Capitoline.
The hills were easier to defend and stayed dry when the Tiber flooded the low ground between them.
Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, became Rome’s port, through which grain and other goods reached the city.

title: The Etruscans
description: Rome’s powerful northern neighbors, whose kings, symbols and rituals shaped early Rome.

facts.text: The Etruscans lived in Etruria, the region north of Rome in what is now Tuscany.
The Etruscans were organized in independent cities and were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy.
The Etruscan language is unrelated to Latin and is still only partly understood.
According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans.
The fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe carried before Roman officials as a sign of authority, came from the Etruscans.
Romans learned haruspicy, reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals, from the Etruscans.

title: The seven kings
description: Tradition counts seven kings from 753 to 509 BCE, chosen with the approval of the Senate and people.

facts.text: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud, ruling from 753 to 509 BCE.
Roman kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says most kings were chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people.
Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and calendar.
Servius Tullius, the sixth king, was credited with the first census, which organized citizens by wealth.
The Roman Senate began as a council of elders advising the king.

title: Roman religion
description: Correct ritual kept the peace of the gods, from household spirits to Jupiter’s temple, Vesta’s fire and augury.

facts.text: Before major public decisions Romans consulted augurs, priests who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds; unfavorable signs could delay public business.
The Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, which was never allowed to go out.
Roman households honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a household shrine.
Roman religion stressed performing rituals correctly; the aim was to keep the pax deorum, peace with the gods.
Rome’s greatest temple, on the Capitoline Hill, was dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods, together with Juno and Minerva.

title: The Roman family
description: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants; the familia included the whole household.

facts.text: The paterfamilias, the oldest living male of a family, held legal power over his children and grandchildren, even as adults.
In early Roman law this power, patria potestas, in theory included the power of life and death over family members.
A Roman familia meant the whole household, including the enslaved people who lived and worked in it.
Noble Roman families kept wax masks of their ancestors and carried them in funeral processions.
A Roman man’s name usually had three parts, as in Gaius Julius Caesar: a personal name, a clan name and a family branch name.

title: The end of the kings
description: Tarquin the Proud was expelled in 509 BCE after the Lucretia scandal, and Romans swore never to have a king again.

facts.text: Tarquin the Proud, the seventh king, was remembered as a tyrant who ruled by force and ignored the Senate.
According to Roman tradition, the assault on the noblewoman Lucretia by the king’s son led to an uprising against the monarchy.
According to Roman tradition, the Romans, led by Lucius Junius Brutus, expelled their king in 509 BCE and ended the monarchy.
Afterwards the title rex, king, was so hated in Rome that even its most powerful later leaders avoided it.
Brutus had the Romans swear never again to allow anyone to be king in Rome.

title: How Rome began
description: A strategic river site, merging Latin villages, Etruscan influence and founding legends together explain early Rome.

facts.text: Early Rome’s rise combined a strategic site on the Tiber, Latin villages that merged into a town, strong Etruscan influence, and founding legends Romans used to explain who they were.

title: The Roman Republic
description: A state run by elected officials with limited terms, the “Senate and People of Rome.”

facts.text: The word republic comes from the Latin res publica, “the public thing”: a state run by elected officials rather than a king.
In the Republic, citizens elected officials called magistrates, who held power for a limited term.
Romans called their state SPQR, Senatus Populusque Romanus: “the Senate and People of Rome.”
Only adult male citizens could vote in the Republic; women, enslaved people and foreigners could not.
The Roman Republic lasted from 509 BCE until Augustus took sole power in 27 BCE.

title: Consuls
description: Two consuls, elected each year, led Rome and its armies; each could block the other.

facts.text: Consuls commanded Rome’s armies in war.
Romans identified each year by the names of its two consuls.
In an emergency Rome could appoint a dictator with supreme power for at most six months.
The Republic was led by two consuls, elected each year, each of whom could block the other’s actions.
Consuls served for one year, so no leader held supreme power for long.

title: The Senate
description: Former magistrates, usually for life, whose advice on war, diplomacy and money was almost always followed.

facts.text: In the Republic the Senate was made up of former magistrates, who usually served for life.
The Senate had about 300 members for most of the Republic.
The Senate formally only gave advice, but its advice was almost always followed, especially on foreign policy and finance.
The Senate usually met in the Curia, a building in the Roman Forum.

title: The Conflict of the Orders
description: Plebeians won political rights from the patricians over about two centuries, using walkouts as leverage.

facts.text: Patricians were members of Rome’s old aristocratic families; plebeians were the rest of the citizens.
In the early Republic, patricians held the magistracies and the priesthoods.
In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians walked out of Rome in protest, a “secession,” refusing to work or fight until they won concessions.
The plebeians’ struggle for political rights, lasting about two centuries, is called the Conflict of the Orders.
From 367 BCE one of the two consuls could be a plebeian.
In 287 BCE the Hortensian law made the votes of the plebeian assembly binding on all Romans, ending the Conflict of the Orders.

title: The Twelve Tables
description: Rome’s first written laws, displayed in the Forum around 450 BCE so everyone could know them.

facts.text: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote down its laws in the Twelve Tables, displayed publicly in the Forum.
Plebeians demanded written laws so that patrician judges could no longer interpret unwritten custom as they pleased.
The Twelve Tables covered everyday matters such as debt, property, family and damage to others.
Centuries later, Cicero recalled memorizing the Twelve Tables as a boy at school, though he noted that boys no longer did so in his day.
The original tablets were lost, probably when the Gauls sacked Rome; the laws survive only in later quotations.

title: Tribunes of the plebs
description: Plebeian officials who could veto any magistrate and who were sacrosanct.

facts.text: The tribunes of the plebs were officials elected by plebeians to protect them from abuses by magistrates.
The number of tribunes of the plebs eventually rose to ten.
Tribunes were sacrosanct: harming one was a religious crime.
A tribune’s door was expected to stay open day and night so that any plebeian could ask for help.
A tribune could block the act of any magistrate by declaring “Veto,” Latin for “I forbid.”

title: Cincinnatus and civic virtue
description: The Roman ideal of the citizen who serves in a crisis and then gives power back.

facts.text: In 458 BCE, according to tradition, the Senate made Cincinnatus dictator to rescue a trapped Roman army, and messengers found him plowing his farm.
Cincinnatus won the war and resigned as dictator after about 16 days, returning to his farm.
Romans prized the mos maiorum, “the custom of the ancestors”: duty, discipline and service to the state.
The American city of Cincinnati is named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which took its name from Cincinnatus.

title: The Gallic sack of Rome
description: Around 390 BCE Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome; afterwards the city built a great stone wall.

facts.text: In about 390 BCE (387 by some counts) Gauls led by Brennus defeated a Roman army at the Allia River and sacked Rome.
According to Livy, when Romans protested the ransom, Brennus threw his sword onto the scales and said “Vae victis”: woe to the conquered.
Legend says the sacred geese of Juno warned the defenders of the Capitoline of a night attack by the Gauls.
After the Gallic sack, Rome built a strong stone wall around the city, later called the Servian Wall.

title: Conquering Italy
description: Through the Samnite Wars, roads like the Via Appia and a network of allies, Rome came to control Italy by about 264 BCE.

facts.text: In the Samnite Wars (343–290 BCE) Rome fought the hill peoples of central and southern Italy for control of the peninsula.
By about 264 BCE Rome controlled nearly all of the Italian peninsula south of the Po Valley.
The Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE, was Rome’s first great road, built to move armies quickly to the south.
King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Roman armies but at such cost that a “Pyrrhic victory” now means a win that costs too much.
Rome bound defeated Italian peoples as allies who supplied soldiers rather than tribute, and granted some of them citizenship.

title: How the Republic worked
description: Consuls, Senate and assemblies each checked the others, a “mixed constitution” admired by Polybius.

facts.text: Roman citizens met in assemblies to elect magistrates and pass laws.
Polybius, a Greek historian taken to Rome as a hostage, wrote his history to explain how Rome came to dominate the Mediterranean world.
The Greek historian Polybius praised Rome’s government as a mix of monarchy (the consuls), aristocracy (the Senate) and democracy (the assemblies), each checking the others.

title: Carthage
description: A Phoenician trading city in North Africa that ruled the western Mediterranean’s seas and clashed with Rome over Sicily.

facts.text: Carthage was founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BCE, on the coast of what is now Tunisia.
Carthage grew rich from trade and became the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean.
Rome and Carthage first went to war in 264 BCE over control of Sicily.
The wars are called Punic from the Latin Punicus, meaning Phoenician.

title: The First Punic War
description: Rome built a navy, used the corvus boarding bridge, and won Sicily, its first province, in 241 BCE.

facts.text: The First Punic War lasted from 264 to 241 BCE.
Rome, which had little experience at sea, built a large war fleet during the First Punic War.
Roman ships used the corvus, a boarding bridge with a spike, to turn sea battles into fights between soldiers.
After winning the First Punic War, Rome took Sicily, its first overseas province.

title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
description: In 218 BCE Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps with elephants to invade Italy, starting the Second Punic War.

facts.text: The Second Punic War (218–201 BCE) was sparked when Hannibal, a Carthaginian general based in Spain, attacked Saguntum, a Roman ally. He then invaded Italy.
In 218 BCE Hannibal led his army, including war elephants, from Spain over the Alps into Italy.
Hannibal lost many men on the march, but most of his elephants survived the Alps (nearly all died in the cold soon after). He reached Italy and won early victories.
Hannibal fought in Italy for about 15 years without being driven out.
According to tradition, Hannibal’s father made him swear as a boy never to be a friend of Rome.

title: Cannae
description: In 216 BCE Hannibal encircled and destroyed a larger Roman army, yet Rome refused to make peace.

facts.text: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal surrounded and destroyed a much larger Roman army.
At Cannae, Hannibal let his center fall back while his wings and cavalry closed around the Romans: a double envelopment.
Ancient sources report Roman losses at Cannae in the tens of thousands, one of the worst defeats in Roman history.
Cannae is still studied by military historians and officers as the classic example of encirclement.
Even after Cannae, Rome refused to make peace with Hannibal.

title: Fabius the Delayer
description: Fabius wore Hannibal down by avoiding battle; Rome’s loyal allies starved him of reinforcements.

facts.text: Fabius Maximus avoided pitched battles with Hannibal, instead shadowing his army and cutting off his supplies.
Fabius’s strategy earned him the nickname Cunctator, “the Delayer,” first as an insult and later as praise.
A “Fabian strategy” still means wearing down a stronger enemy by avoiding a decisive battle.
Most of Rome’s Italian allies stayed loyal during Hannibal’s invasion, denying him the reinforcements he needed.

title: Scipio and Zama
description: Scipio took Spain, invaded Africa and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE, ending the Second Punic War.

facts.text: Publius Cornelius Scipio drove the Carthaginians out of Spain and then invaded Africa, forcing Hannibal to return home.
Scipio defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, winning the Second Punic War.
For his victory, Scipio was given the name Africanus.
After Zama, Carthage lost its overseas territories and most of its fleet and paid Rome a huge indemnity.

title: Rome turns east
description: Rome defeated Macedon and came to dominate Greece, while Greek culture transformed Rome.

facts.text: In a series of wars against the kingdom of Macedon, ending in 148 BCE, Rome came to control Greece.
In 196 BCE the Roman general Flamininus proclaimed the Greek cities free, yet Roman influence over them kept growing.
Greek art, literature and philosophy deeply shaped Roman culture; the poet Horace wrote that captive Greece took its fierce conqueror captive.
In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Greek city of Corinth.

title: The destruction of Carthage
description: Urged on by Cato, Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE and made its land the province of Africa.

facts.text: The senator Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches with the demand that Carthage must be destroyed.
The Third Punic War (149–146 BCE) ended with Rome capturing and destroying Carthage.
Carthage’s territory became the Roman province of Africa.
The story that the Romans sowed salt on Carthage’s fields is a much later invention.
Carthage was later refounded as a Roman colony and became one of the great cities of the empire.

title: The legion
description: Citizen soldiers in flexible maniples and three lines, armed with the gladius and pilum.

facts.text: In the Republic a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry.
Republican legions fought in maniples, small flexible units arranged in three lines.
The three lines were the hastati (the youngest men), the principes, and the triarii (the veterans).
Legionaries carried a short stabbing sword, the gladius, and heavy throwing javelins called pila.
The pilum's long, thin iron shank could bend or lodge in a shield, so an enemy could not easily throw it back, though historians debate whether bending was deliberate.
In the earlier Republic, legionaries were property-owning citizens who supplied their own equipment.

title: Master of the Mediterranean
description: By 146 BCE the Punic and Macedonian wars had made Rome the Mediterranean’s dominant power, ruling provinces through governors.

facts.text: By 146 BCE, after the Punic and Macedonian wars, Rome was the dominant power of the whole Mediterranean.
Rome ruled its new overseas lands as provinces run by governors, beginning with Sicily.

title: The Gracchi
description: Two tribunes who tried to give land to poor citizens and were killed, bringing violence into Roman politics.

facts.text: By the 2nd century BCE, wealthy Romans had built huge estates worked by enslaved people, while many small farmers lost their land.
Tiberius Gracchus was killed by a mob of senators and their supporters, the first great outbreak of political bloodshed in Rome in centuries.
His brother Gaius Gracchus pushed wider reforms, including cheap grain for citizens, and was killed in 121 BCE.
The deaths of the Gracchi showed that political disputes in Rome could now be settled by violence.
In 133 BCE the tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposed giving public land to poor citizens.

title: Marius and the army
description: Marius opened the legions to the landless poor, who then looked to their generals rather than the Senate.

facts.text: Gaius Marius was elected consul an unprecedented seven times.
Marius enrolled poor citizens without property in the army, equipped and paid by the state.
Marius defeated the invading Cimbri and Teutones, Germanic peoples, in 102 and 101 BCE.
Marius made the silver eagle, the aquila, the standard of every legion.
After Marius, soldiers increasingly looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired.

title: Sulla
description: The first general to march on Rome; as dictator without a time limit he killed enemies by proscription.

facts.text: Sulla and Marius, and their supporters, fought a civil war for control of Rome.
Sulla took the dictatorship with no time limit, reformed the constitution to strengthen the Senate, and then retired.
As dictator, Sulla published proscription lists of enemies who could be killed and their property seized.
In 88 BCE Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, something no Roman general had done before.

title: Spartacus
description: A gladiator who led a huge slave revolt from 73 BCE until Crassus crushed it in 71 BCE.

facts.text: In 73 BCE Spartacus, a Thracian gladiator, escaped from a gladiator school at Capua and began a slave revolt.
The rebel army of escaped slaves grew to tens of thousands and defeated several Roman forces.
Marcus Crassus crushed the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BCE.
Some 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way.
Spartacus later became a symbol of resistance to oppression.

title: Pompey the Great
description: A general of extraordinary commands who swept the pirates from the sea and reorganized the East.

facts.text: Pompey first rose to fame as a young commander fighting for Sulla.
Pompey received extraordinary commands that gave him power over huge areas for years at a time.
In 67 BCE Pompey cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in about three months.
Pompey defeated King Mithridates and reorganized the eastern Mediterranean, making Syria a Roman province and capturing Jerusalem in 63 BCE.
Pompey took the name Magnus, “the Great,” in imitation of Alexander the Great.

title: Cicero and Catiline
description: The great orator, consul in 63 BCE, exposed Catiline’s plot and executed conspirators without trial.

facts.text: Cicero was a “new man,” the first in his family to reach the Senate, and became Rome’s greatest orator.
Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE.
As consul, Cicero exposed a conspiracy by Catiline to seize power and denounced him in a series of famous speeches.
Cicero had several conspirators executed without trial, a decision that later led to his exile.
Hundreds of Cicero’s letters survive, making him the best-documented person of the late Republic.

title: The First Triumvirate
description: The 60 BCE alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus, which broke apart after Julia’s and Crassus’s deaths.

facts.text: In 60 BCE Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an informal alliance, later called the First Triumvirate.
Each partner gained something: Caesar a consulship, Pompey land for his veterans, Crassus favors for his allies.
Pompey married Caesar’s daughter Julia, whose death in 54 BCE weakened the bond between the two men.
Crassus was killed in 53 BCE after a disastrous defeat by the Parthians at Carrhae.

title: Caesar in Gaul
description: Caesar conquered Gaul in 58–50 BCE, beat Vercingetorix at Alesia and gained a loyal veteran army.

facts.text: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul between 58 and 50 BCE.
At Alesia in 52 BCE, Caesar defeated the Gallic leader Vercingetorix.
Caesar wrote his own account, the Commentaries on the Gallic War, describing himself in the third person.
The conquest of Gaul gave Caesar enormous wealth and a veteran army loyal to him.
Caesar also led two expeditions to Britain, in 55 and 54 BCE.

title: Crossing the Rubicon
description: In 49 BCE Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy, starting a civil war he won at Pharsalus.

facts.text: The Rubicon, a small river, marked the boundary between Caesar’s province and Italy; a general had to leave his army behind before crossing it.
Caesar is said to have declared “alea iacta est”: the die is cast.
Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in Greece in 48 BCE; Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered there.
“Crossing the Rubicon” now means passing a point of no return.
In January 49 BCE Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army, starting a civil war.

title: The Ides of March
description: Made dictator for life, Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE, but his death did not save the Republic.

facts.text: In 44 BCE Julius Caesar was made dictator for life.
Marcus Brutus claimed descent from the Brutus who had expelled Rome’s last king.
The conspirators hoped to restore the Republic, but Caesar’s murder led to more civil war instead.
On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate by conspirators led by Brutus and Cassius.

title: Octavian, Caesar’s heir
description: Caesar’s adopted heir used his name, the Second Triumvirate and victory at Philippi to build his power.

facts.text: Caesar’s will adopted his 18-year-old great-nephew Octavian as his son and heir.
Octavian took the name Gaius Julius Caesar and used it to win over Caesar’s soldiers and supporters.
In 43 BCE Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate, an alliance given legal power for five years.
The triumvirs revived proscriptions; Cicero, who had attacked Antony in fierce speeches, was killed in 43 BCE.
At Philippi in 42 BCE, Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, who both took their own lives.

title: Antony and Cleopatra
description: Mark Antony ruled the East in alliance with Cleopatra, giving Octavian a foreign enemy to fight.

facts.text: After Philippi, Mark Antony took charge of Rome’s eastern provinces and allied with Cleopatra.
Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Egypt’s Ptolemaic dynasty, a Greek-speaking family descended from a general of Alexander the Great.
Cleopatra had earlier been Julius Caesar’s ally and lover, and had a son, Caesarion, whom she said was Caesar’s.
Antony married Octavian’s sister Octavia in 40 BCE, but later left her for Cleopatra.
In 34 BCE, in the Donations of Alexandria, Antony gave Roman lands in the East to Cleopatra and her children.
Octavian portrayed Antony as a traitor under the spell of a foreign queen, turning opinion in Rome against him.

title: The Battle of Actium
description: Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE, leaving Octavian sole master of Rome.

facts.text: In 32 BCE Rome declared war on Cleopatra, not on Antony, so the conflict looked like a foreign war rather than another civil war.
Marcus Agrippa, Octavian’s closest friend, was his leading general and admiral, and commanded his fleet at Actium.
On 2 September 31 BCE, Octavian’s fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, off western Greece.
In 30 BCE, as Octavian took Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra both took their own lives.
After Actium, Octavian was the sole master of the Roman world.
Egypt became a Roman province under Octavian’s personal control, and its grain helped feed Rome.

title: Augustus and the Principate
description: Augustus ruled as princeps, keeping the Republic’s forms while holding the real power.

facts.text: Under Augustus the Senate, consuls and elections continued, but he controlled most of the legions and the key frontier provinces.
Historians call the system Augustus created the Principate, from princeps.
Augustus ruled until his death in 14 CE, about 40 years as emperor.
Augustus wrote an account of his achievements, the Res Gestae, inscribed on bronze pillars outside his tomb; it lists his victories, buildings and gifts to the Roman people.
Augustus called himself princeps, “first citizen,” and avoided the title of king.
In 27 BCE Octavian claimed to restore the Republic, and the Senate gave him the name Augustus, “the revered one.”

title: The Pax Romana
description: About 200 years of relative peace, from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius, in which trade and cities flourished.

facts.text: The Pax Romana, “Roman peace,” was a period of about 200 years of relative peace and stability across the empire, beginning with Augustus.
During the Pax Romana, safe seas and roads let trade, people and ideas move across the empire, and cities prospered.
The Pax Romana is usually dated from 27 BCE to 180 CE, the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius.
The Pax Romana was not free of war: fighting continued on the frontiers, while the empire’s interior was largely peaceful.

title: Augustus rebuilds Rome
description: Augustus and Agrippa filled Rome with temples and public works that advertised his piety and his peace.

facts.text: According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus boasted that he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.
In the Res Gestae, Augustus says he restored 82 temples in a single year.
Augustus’ buildings advertised his piety and the peace he had brought, linking his rule to Rome’s gods.
Agrippa paid for major public works in Rome, including baths and aqueducts.
The Ara Pacis, the Altar of Augustan Peace, was dedicated in 9 BCE; its carvings show members of Augustus’ family in procession.
Agrippa built the first Pantheon; the domed building standing today is a later rebuilding under the emperor Hadrian.

title: Virgil and the Aeneid
description: Virgil’s epic of the Trojan Aeneas gave Rome a founding poem and Augustus a heroic ancestor.

facts.text: Virgil, who lived from 70 to 19 BCE, is widely regarded as the greatest poet of Augustan Rome.
The Aeneid is an epic poem in 12 books, modeled on Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey.
The Aeneid tells how the Trojan prince Aeneas escaped burning Troy and, guided by fate, came to Italy, where his descendants would found Rome.
The Julian family, including Caesar and Augustus, claimed descent from Aeneas through his son Iulus.
Aeneas is famous for pietas, dutiful devotion to the gods, his family and his country.
Virgil died before finishing the Aeneid and asked for it to be burned; Augustus had it published instead.

title: The Julian calendar
description: Caesar’s 365-day calendar with a leap year; July and August were renamed for Caesar and Augustus.

facts.text: In 46 BCE Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar, with 365 days and a leap day every fourth year, an average of 365.25 days.
Caesar based the calendar reform on the advice of the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria.
The Roman year once began in March, so the month Quintilis meant “fifth month.”
The Julian year was about 11 minutes too long and drifted against the seasons; in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII replaced it with the Gregorian calendar used today.
Quintilis was renamed Julius, our July, in honor of Julius Caesar.
The month Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in honor of Augustus in 8 BCE.

title: The Teutoburg Forest
description: In 9 CE Arminius destroyed three legions under Varus, and Rome settled on the Rhine as its frontier.

facts.text: In 9 CE, Germanic warriors led by Arminius destroyed three Roman legions under the governor Varus in the Teutoburg Forest.
Arminius had served with the Roman army and was trusted by Varus, whom he led into an ambush.
After the disaster, Rome gave up plans to conquer Germany east of the Rhine, which became a lasting frontier.
Archaeologists believe the battlefield lies near Kalkriese in Germany, where Roman weapons and coins have been found.
According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus cried out, “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”

title: From Republic to Empire
description: Violence and loyal armies turned the Republic into one-man rule that kept republican forms.

facts.text: The change from Republic to Empire kept republican forms, such as the Senate and the consuls, while real power passed to one man.
The word emperor comes from imperator, a title Roman soldiers gave to a victorious commander.

title: Tiberius and succession
description: Augustus’ adopted stepson ruled from 14 to 37 CE; with no law of succession, every heir was a gamble.

facts.text: Augustus had no surviving son, and adopted his stepson Tiberius as heir after other chosen successors died.
Tiberius became emperor on Augustus’ death in 14 CE and ruled until 37 CE.
Rome never had a fixed law of succession; each emperor had to choose an heir, often by adoption.
In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri and ruled from there.
While Tiberius was away, Sejanus, commander of the Praetorian Guard, grew powerful until Tiberius had him executed in 31 CE.
The Praetorian Guard was the emperor’s bodyguard, stationed in Rome itself.

title: Caligula
description: A young emperor who began popular and became autocratic; much of his legend comes from hostile writers.

facts.text: Gaius, known as Caligula, became emperor in 37 CE and was murdered by officers of the Praetorian Guard in 41 CE.
Caligula means “little boot,” a nickname soldiers gave him as a child, when he wore a small soldier’s uniform in his father’s camp.
Caligula was popular at first, but his rule soon became autocratic and extravagant.
The story that Caligula planned to make his horse a consul may be a joke or an exaggeration.
Most accounts of Caligula come from later writers hostile to him, so historians treat the wildest stories with caution.

title: Claudius and Britain
description: An emperor few took seriously, Claudius launched the conquest of Britain in 43 CE.

facts.text: After Caligula’s murder, the Praetorian Guard made his uncle Claudius emperor in 41 CE.
Claudius had a limp and a stammer, and his family kept him out of public life; he was a scholar who wrote histories, now lost.
In 43 CE Claudius launched the invasion of Britain, which became a Roman province.
In about 60 CE Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a revolt in Britain that burned London before the Romans crushed it.
Claudius relied on freedmen, formerly enslaved people, as powerful officials.

title: Nero and the Great Fire
description: Nero, emperor from 54 CE, blamed the Christians for the fire of 64 CE; his death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line.

facts.text: Nero, Claudius’ adopted son, became emperor in 54 CE at the age of 16.
In 64 CE a great fire burned in Rome for six days; three of the city’s 14 districts were destroyed and seven more badly damaged.
Nero blamed the Christians in Rome for the fire and had many of them executed.
Nero built a vast palace, the Golden House, on land cleared by the fire.
The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is a later legend: the fiddle did not yet exist, and Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire began.
Facing revolt, Nero took his own life in 68 CE, ending the Julio-Claudian dynasty, the family line of Augustus.

title: The Year of the Four Emperors
description: In 69 CE four men held power in turn, each backed by an army; Vespasian won and founded the Flavian dynasty.

facts.text: In 69 CE, the Year of the Four Emperors, Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each held power in turn.
Each claimant in 69 CE was backed by an army, showing that the legions could make and unmake emperors.
Vespasian, a general commanding in Judaea, won the civil war and founded the Flavian dynasty.
The historian Tacitus wrote that the fall of Nero in 68 CE revealed a secret of empire: an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome.
Vespasian came from a family of modest rank, not the old Roman nobility.

title: The Flavians and the Colosseum
description: Vespasian and his sons ruled from 69 to 96 CE and built the Colosseum on Nero’s palace grounds.

facts.text: In 70 CE Vespasian’s son Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed its Temple.
Titus succeeded Vespasian and was followed by his brother Domitian, whose harsh rule ended with his murder in 96 CE.
Vespasian began the Colosseum, and his son Titus opened it in 80 CE.
The games held to open the Colosseum lasted 100 days.
The Colosseum could hold about 50,000 spectators.
The Colosseum was built on the site of a lake in the grounds of Nero’s Golden House, giving the land back to public use.
The Colosseum’s official name was the Flavian Amphitheatre; the name Colosseum came later, probably from a colossal statue of Nero nearby.
Titus was emperor when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE.

title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
description: The eruption of 79 CE buried Pompeii and preserved an ordinary Roman town for historians.

facts.text: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters to the historian Tacitus; his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died trying to rescue people.
Pompeii was buried under several meters of ash and pumice, which preserved buildings, paintings and everyday objects.
Pompeii’s walls preserve painted notices and scratched graffiti, including election slogans.
In the 1800s, excavators poured plaster into hollows left in the ash by victims’ bodies, making casts of their final positions.
Pompeii gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life.

title: Trajan
description: The first emperor from outside Italy conquered Dacia and brought the empire to its greatest extent in 117 CE.

facts.text: Trajan, born in Spain, was the first emperor from outside Italy; he ruled from 98 to 117 CE.
The Senate gave Trajan the title Optimus, “the best.”
Trajan conquered Dacia, roughly modern Romania, in two wars ending in 106 CE.
Trajan’s Column in Rome shows the Dacian wars in a spiral band of carvings winding from base to top.
Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest extent, in 117 CE, after he conquered lands as far as Mesopotamia.

title: Hadrian and his wall
description: Hadrian stopped expanding, toured the frontiers and fortified them, most famously in northern Britain.

facts.text: Hadrian, Trajan’s successor, ruled from 117 to 138 CE and gave up some of Trajan’s eastern conquests.
Hadrian spent much of his reign traveling through the provinces, inspecting the armies and frontiers.
Hadrian’s Wall, begun in 122 CE, ran about 118 km across northern Britain.
Hadrian loved Greek culture and was the first emperor regularly portrayed with a full beard, in the Greek style.
Hadrian’s Wall had small forts about every Roman mile, and larger forts along its length.

title: The Five Good Emperors
description: From 96 to 180 CE, emperors chosen by adoption gave Rome its most stable era; Commodus ended it.

facts.text: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 96 to 180 CE, are known as the Five Good Emperors.
None of the first four Good Emperors left a surviving son, so each passed power to an adopted adult heir, though even ancient writers doubted that Trajan really adopted Hadrian before he died.
The historian Edward Gibbon called this era the time when the human race was most happy and prosperous.
Marcus Aurelius, a Stoic philosopher, wrote his private reflections, the Meditations, while on campaign.
A deadly epidemic, the Antonine Plague, swept the empire from about 165 CE.
Marcus Aurelius was succeeded by his own son Commodus, whose disastrous reign ended the era.

title: Life in the city of Rome
description: A city of perhaps a million, where most lived in crowded insulae and public life centered on the Forum.

facts.text: By the time of Augustus, the city of Rome had perhaps around 1 million inhabitants, the largest city in the Western world.
Most people in Rome lived in insulae, crowded apartment blocks several stories high, usually without running water or private baths.
In insulae the upper floors were the cheapest, and fire and collapse were constant dangers.
Augustus set a height limit of about 20 meters for new buildings in Rome.
Wealthy Romans lived in a domus, a private house built around an open hall called the atrium.
The Forum was the center of Roman public life, with temples, law courts, markets and platforms for speeches.
Augustus created the vigiles, a force of freedmen who fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.

title: Slavery in Rome
description: Enslaved people did every kind of work; many were freed, and freed slaves of citizens became citizens.

facts.text: Enslaved people made up a large share of the population of Roman Italy.
People were enslaved through war, piracy and trade, and children born to enslaved mothers were enslaved too.
Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own.
Enslaved people did every kind of work, from mines and farms to households, and some served as teachers, doctors and secretaries.
Romans often freed enslaved people, a practice called manumission.
A person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a Roman citizen, and their children had full rights.

title: Bread and circuses
description: Free grain and public games kept Rome’s crowds fed, entertained and loyal to the rulers who paid.

facts.text: The poet Juvenal complained that the Roman people, who once handed out commands, now wanted only two things: bread and circuses.
Rome gave free grain to many citizens living in the city; under Augustus about 200,000 people received it.
Public games, ludi, began as religious festivals and grew into huge free entertainments.
Emperors and politicians paid for games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm.

title: Gladiators
description: Mostly enslaved or condemned fighters in set types; many bouts ended without a death, and the thumb signal is uncertain.

facts.text: Gladiator fights probably began as funeral games to honor the dead, first recorded in Rome in 264 BCE.
Most gladiators were enslaved people, prisoners of war or condemned criminals, but some free men volunteered.
Gladiators fought in types with set equipment, such as the net-and-trident retiarius against the helmeted secutor.
Gladiators were expensive to train, and many fights did not end in death: a beaten fighter could be spared.
Roman writers mention a “turned thumb” deciding a gladiator’s fate, but its exact meaning is unknown.

title: Chariot racing
description: Rome’s most popular spectacle, raced by four color factions at the vast Circus Maximus.

facts.text: The Circus Maximus, Rome’s great racetrack, could hold about 150,000 spectators.
Charioteers raced for four factions, the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, each with passionate fans.
A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina.
The most prestigious races used four-horse chariots, called quadrigae.
Successful charioteers could become rich and famous.
In 532 CE fans of the Blues and Greens rioted together in Constantinople in the Nika revolt, nearly toppling the emperor Justinian.

title: The Roman baths
description: Heated public baths with hot, warm and cold rooms were cheap social centers for all classes.

facts.text: Large public baths, thermae, had hot, warm and cold rooms: the caldarium, tepidarium and frigidarium.
Baths were heated by the hypocaust: hot air from furnaces flowed under raised floors and through the walls.
The Baths of Caracalla, opened in the 3rd century CE, could serve about 1,600 bathers at a time.
Instead of soap, bathers oiled their skin and scraped it clean with a curved metal tool, the strigil.
Baths were social centers where Romans exercised, talked, did business and relaxed, and entry was cheap.

title: What Romans ate
description: Grain, oil and wine for most; reclining banquets for the rich; garum fish sauce for everyone.

facts.text: Most Romans lived on grain, eaten as porridge or bread, with olive oil, wine, vegetables and beans.
Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was one of the most popular seasonings in the Roman world.
Garum was made in coastal factories, especially in Spain, and shipped around the empire in clay jars called amphorae.
Wealthy Romans held dinner parties in the triclinium, reclining on couches around a table.
A Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius survives, with many recipes that use fish sauce.
Romans had no tomatoes, potatoes or maize; these came from the Americas more than a thousand years later.
Street counters called thermopolia sold hot food to city dwellers, many of whom had no kitchen at home.

title: Latin and its descendants
description: Rome’s language spread west, became the Romance languages and still fills English.

facts.text: Latin was first spoken in Latium, the region around Rome.
Everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin, gradually developed into the Romance languages.
Latin remained the language of the Western Church, law and scholarship for centuries after the Western Empire fell.
Romanian descends from the Latin spoken in the Roman province of Dacia and the lands around it.
Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials, while Greek stayed the common language of the East.
The Romance languages include Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.
English is not a Romance language, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French.

title: Roman women
description: Women could own property and wield influence, but could not vote or hold office.

facts.text: Roman women could not vote or hold political office.
Under early Roman law a woman needed a male guardian for legal matters, though the rule weakened over time.
Many Roman women owned property, ran businesses and inherited wealth.
Livia, the wife of Augustus, was one of the most influential people in Rome.
Roman daughters usually took a feminine form of the family name: Julius Caesar’s daughter was simply Julia.
Roman girls from elite families were often married in their early to mid teens, usually to older men; most other girls probably married in their late teens.

title: Everyday Rome
description: Cramped homes pushed life into public spaces, bound together by patrons, gods, bread and games.

facts.text: Life in Rome combined grand public spaces, such as baths, forums and arenas, with crowded and risky housing for most people.
Because homes were cramped, much of Roman life happened in public: in the streets, baths, forums and arenas.
Many Romans were clients of a wealthy patron, greeting him in the morning in return for help and protection.

title: Roman roads
description: A vast network of layered, drained, straight roads built for the army and used by everyone.

facts.text: At its height the Roman road network included more than 80,000 km of main roads.
Major Roman roads were built in layers: a foundation of large stones, then gravel or rubble, topped with paving stones.
Roman roads ran as straight as the ground allowed and were cambered, curved slightly, so rainwater drained off.
Milestones along Roman roads marked distances in Roman miles of 1,000 paces.
Roman roads were built first for the army, letting legions march quickly, but they also carried trade, officials and the imperial post.

title: Aqueducts
description: Gravity carried water along gentle slopes, mostly underground, to supply Roman cities.

facts.text: Aqueducts carried water by gravity, along a gentle, steady downhill slope from springs in the hills.
Most of an aqueduct’s length ran underground or at ground level; the famous arches carried it across valleys.
Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius, who also began the Appian Way.
By the 3rd century CE, 11 aqueducts supplied the city of Rome.
The Pont du Gard in southern France is a surviving three-tier aqueduct bridge about 49 m high.
Frontinus, Rome’s water commissioner around 97 CE, wrote a book about the city’s aqueducts.

title: Roman concrete
description: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater, shaped domes and has lasted two thousand years.

facts.text: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash, called pozzolana, and chunks of rock or brick.
Pozzolana is named after Pozzuoli, near Naples, where the volcanic ash was dug.
Concrete made with volcanic ash could set even underwater, which let Romans build harbors in the sea.
Concrete let Romans build arches, vaults and domes on a scale never seen before.
Roman concrete walls were usually faced with brick or stone, so the concrete core was hidden.
A 2023 study found that lumps of lime in Roman concrete could react with water to seal cracks, helping it last.

title: The Pantheon
description: Hadrian’s temple has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit by a single open oculus.

facts.text: Pantheon means “of all the gods.”
The Pantheon’s dome, about 43 m across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
An open hole at the top of the dome, the oculus, about 8 m wide, is the building’s only source of natural light.
The height from the floor to the top of the Pantheon’s dome equals the dome’s diameter, so a complete sphere would fit inside.
The Pantheon’s dome gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up.
In 609 CE the Pantheon became a Christian church, which helped it survive intact.

title: Running the provinces
description: Governors, taxes and local elites ran a vast empire with very few Roman officials.

facts.text: Augustus split the provinces: peaceful ones had governors chosen by the Senate, while frontier provinces with armies were run by his own deputies.
Provinces paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation.
In the Republic, tax collection was often contracted out to private companies of publicani, who were notorious for abuses.
Rome ran its provinces with few officials, relying on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes.
Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE.

title: Roman citizenship
description: Citizenship spread from Rome to Italy and the provinces until Caracalla extended it to almost all free people in 212.

facts.text: Roman citizens had legal privileges, such as the right to appeal to Rome and protection from certain punishments.
During the Social War of 91–88 BCE, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies, first to those who stayed loyal and then to the rest, which helped end the revolt.
Citizenship spread through the provinces by grants to towns, to individuals and to soldiers.
Non-citizen soldiers, the auxiliaries, received Roman citizenship after about 25 years of service.
In 212 CE the emperor Caracalla granted citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.
According to the Book of Acts, Paul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, used his right to appeal to the emperor.

title: Roman law
description: From the Twelve Tables to Justinian’s code, Roman law became the base of the world’s civil law systems.

facts.text: Roman legal experts, the jurists, wrote opinions that developed and explained the law.
Roman jurists held that the burden of proof rests on the person who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it.
Many legal terms in English are Latin, such as alibi, meaning “elsewhere.”
In the 6th century CE the emperor Justinian had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.”
Justinian’s code shaped the civil law systems used across continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries.

title: Money and trade
description: Silver coins carried the emperor’s face; amphorae carried wine, oil and garum across a connected Mediterranean.

facts.text: The denarius, a silver coin, was the standard Roman coin for centuries.
Roman coins carried the emperor’s portrait and short messages, spreading his image across the empire.
Wine, olive oil and fish sauce moved around the Mediterranean in amphorae, clay jars made for shipping.
Monte Testaccio in Rome is an artificial hill made of fragments of millions of broken olive oil amphorae.
Roman traders sailed to India, and Chinese silk reached Rome through many middlemen along the Silk Road.
Over time emperors reduced the silver in the denarius, and by the 3rd century CE it held very little.

title: Life on the frontier
description: Forts, auxiliaries and the towns beside them held the limes, as the Vindolanda letters reveal.

facts.text: The fortified frontier of the Roman Empire was called the limes.
Much of the frontier was held by auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces.
Roman forts followed a standard plan: a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates and a headquarters building at the center.
Civilian settlements grew up beside frontier forts, with traders, craftsmen and soldiers’ families.
At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found hundreds of wooden writing tablets, including a birthday invitation from one commander’s wife to another.

title: How Rome held an empire
description: Roads, citizenship, law, trade and a shared army bound the empire together, not force alone.

facts.text: Rome held its empire together with roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade, not by force alone.
Historians call the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces Romanization; towns across the West built forums, baths and amphitheaters on the Roman model.

title: The Crisis of the Third Century
description: From 235 to 284 CE, rapid-fire emperors, invasions, plague and inflation nearly broke the empire apart.

facts.text: From 235 to 284 CE, the Crisis of the Third Century, the empire suffered civil wars, invasions, plague and economic trouble.
In about 50 years of crisis there were more than 20 emperors, most of whom were killed in office.
In 260 CE the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I, the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.
For a time the empire split into three: a breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, Rome in the middle, and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia in the east.
The emperor Aurelian reunited the empire in the 270s and built new walls around Rome.

title: Diocletian and the Tetrarchy
description: Diocletian ended the crisis with rule by four emperors, smaller provinces and a split between East and West.

facts.text: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis.
Diocletian created the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars.
The Tetrarchy was meant to put an emperor near every threatened frontier and give the empire a planned succession.
Diocletian split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command.
In 301 CE Diocletian’s Edict on Maximum Prices tried, and failed, to stop inflation by fixing prices.
In 305 CE Diocletian retired, the first Roman emperor to step down voluntarily, to his palace at Split in modern Croatia.

title: The first Christians
description: A Jewish movement from Judaea spread through the empire’s cities, carried by its roads, peace and Greek.

facts.text: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher executed by crucifixion in Judaea under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate.
Paul of Tarsus spread Christianity to non-Jews in cities around the eastern Mediterranean.
Christianity spread mainly in cities, helped by Roman roads, peace and the common Greek language of the East.
Christians worshiped one God and refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods or to the emperor.
Christian communities were led by bishops and cared for their poor, widows and sick.

title: Persecution
description: Local and sporadic at first, persecution became empire-wide under Decius and harshest under Diocletian.

facts.text: For most of the first two centuries, persecution of Christians was local and sporadic, not constant.
Pliny the Younger, as a governor, asked Trajan how to treat Christians; Trajan replied that they should not be hunted out, but punished if accused and they refused to recant.
In 250 CE the emperor Decius ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods, the first empire-wide persecution.
The Great Persecution under Diocletian, from 303 CE, was the harshest the Christians faced.
Refusing to sacrifice to the gods and the emperor looked like disloyalty, and Romans feared it would break the peace with the gods.
Christians who died for their faith were honored as martyrs, from a Greek word meaning “witness.”

title: Constantine
description: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge, granted Christians tolerance and called the Council of Nicaea.

facts.text: In 312 CE Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome.
Christian writers said Constantine saw a sign before the battle and had his soldiers fight under a Christian symbol.
In 313 CE, the Edict of Milan granted religious tolerance to Christians throughout the empire.
By 324 CE Constantine had defeated his last rival and ruled the whole empire alone.
In 325 CE Constantine called the Council of Nicaea, a meeting of bishops that agreed a common statement of Christian belief.
Constantine was baptized only on his deathbed, in 337 CE.

title: Constantinople
description: Constantine’s new Rome on the Bosporus, closer to the frontiers, lasted as a capital for over a thousand years.

facts.text: Constantinople stood on the Bosporus, the strait between Europe and Asia, controlling the route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
The new capital was closer than Rome to the threatened Danube and eastern frontiers.
Constantinople was built as a new Rome, with its own senate, forums and a great hippodrome for chariot racing.
Constantinople is today Istanbul, in Turkey.
Constantine dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium in 330 CE.

title: Julian the Apostate
description: Constantine’s nephew tried to restore the old gods, but died in Persia after less than two years.

facts.text: Julian, Constantine’s nephew, became sole emperor in 361 CE.
Julian rejected Christianity and tried to restore worship of the traditional gods.
Christians called him Julian the Apostate: an apostate is someone who abandons their faith.
Julian was the last Roman emperor to follow the traditional gods.
Julian banned Christians from teaching classical literature.
Julian was killed on campaign against Persia in 363 CE, and his religious program died with him.

title: A Christian empire
description: Under Theodosius, Christianity became the official religion and the old cults were shut down.

facts.text: In 380 CE, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the empire.
In the 390s Theodosius banned sacrifices and closed temples.
The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally said to have ended in 393 CE under Theodosius.
In the 390s the sacred fire of Vesta was put out and the Vestal Virgins were disbanded.
Bishop Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica, showing the church’s new power.
Theodosius was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire; after his death in 395 CE it was divided between his two sons.

title: The Battle of Adrianople
description: In 378 CE Goths who had crossed the Danube destroyed a Roman army and killed the emperor Valens.

facts.text: In 376 CE Goths fleeing the Huns were allowed to cross the Danube into the empire.
The Huns, nomadic horsemen from the Eurasian steppes, were pushing west in the 370s, driving other peoples before them.
Mistreated and exploited by Roman officials, the Goths rebelled.
At Adrianople in 378 CE the Goths destroyed a Roman army, and the emperor Valens was killed.
Gothic cavalry arriving during the battle played a decisive part in the Roman defeat.
Afterwards, Gothic groups settled inside the empire as allies under their own leaders, a new and risky arrangement.

title: The empire of 395
description: By 395 the empire was Christian, ruled by distant monarchs, split in two and defended partly by Germanic allies.

facts.text: By 395 CE the empire was Christian, divided into East and West, and defended partly by Germanic allies under their own leaders.
Later emperors ruled more openly as absolute monarchs, surrounded by elaborate court ceremony; historians sometimes call this the Dominate, from dominus, “lord.”

title: The sack of Rome, 410
description: Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 CE, a shock that led Augustine to write The City of God.

facts.text: By 410 CE the western emperor Honorius lived at Ravenna, a city protected by marshes, not in Rome.
Stilicho, the western empire’s leading general, had held the Visigoth leader Alaric off, but he was executed in 408 CE.
In 410 CE the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome, the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in about 800 years.
Alaric’s troops plundered Rome for three days.
The scholar Jerome wrote that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken.
Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God partly to answer pagans who blamed the sack on the abandonment of the old gods.

title: Attila and the Huns
description: Attila extorted gold from the East, was stopped in Gaul in 451 and turned back from Italy in 452.

facts.text: Attila ruled the Huns from 434 to 453 CE, at first jointly with his brother Bleda.
Attila raided the Eastern Empire and forced it to pay him large amounts of gold.
In 451 CE a Roman and Visigothic army under the general Aetius stopped Attila’s invasion of Gaul at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains.
In 452 CE Attila invaded Italy; Pope Leo I met him, and Attila withdrew.
Attila died in 453 CE, and his empire of many peoples soon fell apart.
Christian writers called Attila the “Scourge of God.”

title: 476: the last western emperor
description: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE; historians debate how much actually changed.

facts.text: In 455 CE the Vandals sacked Rome for two weeks.
The word vandalism comes from the Vandals’ name.
In 476 CE the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the young western emperor Romulus Augustulus.
Odoacer did not make himself emperor: he sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king.
Romulus Augustulus bore the names of Rome’s founder and its first emperor; Augustulus means “little Augustus.”
Many historians see 476 CE as a convenient marker rather than a sudden end, since life in Italy went on much as before for many people.

title: Why did Rome fall?
description: Invasions, civil wars and lost revenue broke the West; some historians prefer to speak of transformation.

facts.text: Historians have proposed many different reasons for the fall of the Western Empire.
Pressure from Germanic peoples and the Huns stretched the western army beyond its limits.
Repeated civil wars between Roman generals weakened the West from within.
The Vandals’ capture of Carthage in 439 CE cost the West its richest tax base and a major grain supply.
Edward Gibbon’s The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire blamed, in part, the rise of Christianity and a loss of civic virtue.
Some historians describe the period as a transformation into the kingdoms of medieval Europe rather than a sudden collapse.
The East was richer and more populous than the West, which helps explain why it survived.

title: The Eastern Roman Empire
description: The Greek-speaking “Byzantine” empire called itself Roman and lasted until 1453.

facts.text: Historians call the Eastern Roman Empire the Byzantine Empire, but its people called themselves Romans.
Over time Greek replaced Latin as the language of the eastern empire’s government.
In the 6th century CE, Justinian reconquered Italy and North Africa for a time.
Justinian built the great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, finished in 537 CE.
Sultan Mehmed II led the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 CE.

title: Rome in our laws and governments
description: Senates, vetoes, capitols, balanced constitutions and civil law all come from Rome.

facts.text: The United States Senate takes its name from the Roman Senate.
The United States Capitol is named after Rome’s Capitoline Hill.
The word veto is still used for the power to block laws, as when a US president vetoes a bill.
The framers of the US Constitution studied the Roman Republic and its balance between different parts of government.

title: Rome in our words, calendars and cities
description: Roman towns, grids, columns, mottoes and months still shape the world.

facts.text: Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles.
Many European cities grew from Roman towns or forts, including London, Paris, Cologne and Vienna.
Neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts in buildings across Europe and the Americas.
Latin mottoes still appear on seals and coins, such as “E pluribus unum,” “out of many, one,” on the Great Seal of the United States.

title: How we know about Rome
description: Historians weigh biased texts against inscriptions, coins and archaeology.

facts.text: Much of Roman history comes from ancient writers such as Livy, Tacitus and Suetonius, who had their own sources, purposes and biases.
Huge numbers of Latin inscriptions carved in stone record laws, careers, dedications and epitaphs.
Coins help historians date events and show how emperors wanted to be seen.
Archaeology reveals ordinary lives that writers ignored, from houses and graves to rubbish heaps.

title: The arc of Roman history
description: From 753 BCE to 1453 CE, one thread runs through it: whoever held the army held the state.

facts.text: Roman history spans more than 2,000 years, from the traditional founding in 753 BCE to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 CE.
A recurring pattern in Roman history is that whoever controlled the army controlled the state.
